title: Indigenous Responses to State Expansion from 1750 to 1900

themes.label: Political
themes.tooltip: Colonial expansion provoked a range of political responses from indigenous peoples, including armed resistance, state-building, diplomatic negotiation, and political movements demanding self-governance.

themes.label: Ideas & Beliefs
themes.tooltip: Nationalism, the idea that distinct peoples have a right to self-governance, was adopted by colonized peoples as justification for anticolonial resistance, turning the colonizers’ own ideology against them.

themes.label: Culture & Religion
themes.tooltip: Spiritual resistance movements, the Ghost Dance, Xhosa Cattle-Killing, Mahdist War, demonstrate how religious frameworks provided meaning, community, and hope when military options were exhausted.

tldr: **LO-A: Direct armed resistance, fighting back with force:** Many indigenous peoples chose direct military resistance to colonial conquest. Key examples include the 1857 Rebellion in India (sepoys and civilians against East India Company rule), Samory Touré’s Wassoulou Empire resisting French expansion in West Africa, and the Yaa Asantewaa War (1900) in which the Asante queen mother led Gold Coast resistance to British demands. All ultimately failed against industrial military superiority. **Creating new states, building political structures to resist:** Some communities responded by constructing new, stronger political entities. The Sokoto Caliphate (founded 1804 in present-day Nigeria) unified Hausa city-states under Islamic governance. The Zulu Kingdom under Shaka expanded to become a major regional power that held off British forces at Isandlwana (1879), one of Britain’s worst military defeats. Balkan peoples formed new nation-states as the Ottoman Empire weakened. **Religious and spiritual resistance movements, faith as resistance:** When military options were exhausted, communities often turned to spiritual responses. The Ghost Dance movement (1889–90) among Plains Indians promised that performing the ritual would make settlers disappear and restore indigenous life; it ended at Wounded Knee (1890). The Xhosa Cattle-Killing Movement (1856–57) in southern Africa was a prophetic movement that ultimately destroyed the Xhosa’s capacity for resistance. The Mahdist War in Sudan (1881–98) combined religious revival with military resistance to Egyptian-British rule. **Why most resistance failed, the military technology gap:** Industrial weapons, repeating rifles, artillery, Maxim guns, gunboats, created a gap between colonizers and colonized that no amount of courage could bridge. The Maxim gun (1884), the world’s first recoil-operated machine gun, could fire 500 rounds per minute. Hilaire Belloc’s satirical lines captured the asymmetry: “Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim Gun, and they have not.”.
learningObjectives: Explain how and why internal and external factors influenced the process of state building, including anticolonial resistance, from 1750 to 1900

vocabulary.definition: Organized opposition by indigenous or colonized peoples to foreign imperial rule, ranging from armed rebellion to cultural preservation to political mobilization.
vocabulary.importance: A defining feature of the imperial age; demonstrates that colonized peoples were not passive victims but active agents who contested foreign rule in multiple ways.

vocabulary.definition: A major uprising against British East India Company rule in India, involving both sepoys (Indian soldiers) and civilians. Also called the First War of Indian Independence.
vocabulary.importance: Reflected deep resentment of Company rule; led to the end of Company rule and the beginning of the British Raj; a landmark in Indian nationalist memory.

vocabulary.definition: West African Muslim ruler who built the Wassoulou Empire and led prolonged military resistance to French colonial expansion in present-day Guinea and Mali from the 1860s to 1898.
vocabulary.importance: One of the most sustained examples of African military resistance to European colonization; his guerrilla tactics delayed French conquest for decades before his capture.

vocabulary.definition: An uprising in the Asante kingdom (present-day Ghana) led by Queen Mother Yaa Asantewaa against British demands to surrender the Golden Stool, the sacred symbol of Asante sovereignty.
vocabulary.importance: An example of direct resistance that combined political, cultural, and military elements; the British ultimately prevailed, annexing Asante in 1902.

vocabulary.definition: An Islamic state founded by Usman dan Fodio in 1804 in present-day Nigeria, unifying Hausa city-states under Islamic governance through the Fulani Jihad.
vocabulary.importance: Example of a new state created on the periphery as a response to political instability; one of the largest states in 19th-century Africa before British conquest in 1903.

vocabulary.definition: A spiritual movement among Plains Indian peoples (1889–90) based on the teachings of Wovoka, a Paiute prophet, who taught that performing the Ghost Dance would restore indigenous life and make European settlers disappear.
vocabulary.importance: Represents religious/spiritual resistance to colonial conquest; ended at the massacre at Wounded Knee (1890), when U.S. soldiers killed approximately 300 Lakota Sioux.

vocabulary.definition: A religious-military uprising in Sudan led by Muhammad Ahmad (the Mahdi), who declared himself the Expected Mahdi (guided one) and led forces that defeated Egyptian-British forces and held Sudan independently until the Battle of Omdurman (1898).
vocabulary.importance: One of the most successful examples of armed anticolonial resistance; combined Islamic revival with nationalism; eventually suppressed by Kitchener’s British army.

vocabulary.definition: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, who took the name Túpac Amaru II and led the largest indigenous uprising in colonial Latin American history (1780–81) against Spanish rule in Peru.
vocabulary.importance: Mobilized indigenous and mestizo communities against colonial taxation and forced labor; executed by Spanish authorities; remains a powerful symbol of indigenous resistance in Latin America.

preTest.question: Why might some communities respond to colonial pressure by building stronger, larger political entities (like the Sokoto Caliphate or Zulu Kingdom) rather than fighting immediately?
preTest.answer: Larger political entities commanded more resources, soldiers, and diplomatic leverage than scattered individual communities. Building a unified state converted fragmented local resistance into coordinated regional power. The Sokoto Caliphate unified dozens of Hausa city-states under a shared Islamic political framework, giving the new state both military strength and ideological legitimacy. Similarly, Shaka’s Zulu Kingdom absorbed neighboring peoples through conquest and alliance, creating a military force large enough to defeat British forces at Isandlwana (1879). This strategy recognized that individual communities were too small to resist alone but that a larger state might succeed. The tragedy is that even these stronger states eventually fell to the combination of industrial weapons and relentless colonial pressure.

preTest.question: Why might spiritual or religious resistance movements emerge when military resistance has been defeated or is clearly impossible?
preTest.answer: When conventional resistance is futile, when the military gap is too large to bridge, communities facing destruction may turn to spiritual frameworks that offer hope outside the material world. The Ghost Dance promised Plains Indians that performing the ritual would restore their world without military action. The Xhosa Cattle-Killing offered prophetic salvation through sacrifice. These movements emerged not from delusion but from the genuine impossibility of other options: the military fight was over, the land was lost, and yet the community still needed something to believe in and organize around. Religious frameworks also provide community solidarity and meaning during catastrophic loss in ways that purely military thinking cannot.

preTest.question: The 1857 Rebellion in India is sometimes called a “Sepoy Mutiny” and sometimes the “First War of Indian Independence.” What does the naming dispute reveal?
preTest.answer: The naming reveals whose perspective organizes the historical narrative. The British called it a “mutiny”, a breach of military discipline by soldiers who violated their oaths, because from a British colonial perspective, the issue was disorder within a legitimate military chain of command. Indian nationalists called it the “First War of Independence” because from their perspective, it was an uprising against foreign occupation. Both descriptions are accurate about different aspects of the same event: it was simultaneously a military mutiny (soldiers refused orders) and a broad political rebellion (the uprising spread far beyond the military to encompass civilians, landlords, and princes). Which name you use signals which framework you’re applying.

preTest.question: The Zulu Kingdom defeated a British army at Isandlwana in 1879. Why did this victory not ultimately prevent British conquest of Zululand?
preTest.answer: A single military victory, however dramatic, could not overcome the structural asymmetry between an industrial empire and a pre-industrial state. Britain could absorb the loss of 1,300 soldiers, reinforce its army, and return with Maxim guns and artillery. The Zulus could not similarly replace losses or upgrade their weapons. The battle also shocked Britain into sending much larger reinforcements, the defeat at Isandlwana, paradoxically, accelerated the British commitment to conquering Zululand rather than retreating from it. A temporary military success without a path to sustainable advantage couldn’t change the long-term outcome.

preTest.question: Why might nationalism, the belief in a distinct national identity, be a tool of both imperialism and anti-imperialism?
preTest.answer: Nationalism is a political technology that can serve either purpose depending on context. European nationalism drove imperialism by creating competitive pressures among nations to acquire colonies. But the same idea, that distinct peoples have a right to self-governance based on shared identity, culture, and history, could be turned against colonial rule: if Frenchmen had a right to govern themselves, why not Vietnamese? If the Germans had a nation, why not the Indians or the Africans? This is precisely why KC-5.3.III.D notes that nationalism and questions about political authority contributed to anticolonial movements. Colonized peoples used the colonizers’ own ideology against them.

blocks.text: 🎯 The Spectrum of Resistance: More Than Just Armed Revolt

When colonial powers expanded, indigenous peoples did not simply submit. They responded, in dozens of different ways, at different scales, with different strategies. The CED organizes these responses into three overlapping categories: **direct armed resistance**, **creating new states** on the periphery, and **rebellions influenced by religious or spiritual ideas**. Understanding all three is essential for the AP exam.

Before diving in, it’s worth thinking about the range of responses that existed beyond these three categories: diplomatic negotiation (signing treaties, seeking alliances with rival European powers), cultural preservation (hiding or protecting sacred objects, continuing banned practices), economic adaptation (shifting trade relationships to maintain some autonomy), and political accommodation (working within colonial structures to preserve community interests). The three CED categories capture the most dramatic responses, but the full picture is more complex.
⚔️ Direct Armed Resistance: Fighting Back

The most dramatic response to colonial expansion was armed resistance. Across Africa, Asia, and the Americas, indigenous peoples fought against colonial conquest. Most ultimately failed, the combination of industrial weapons, logistical capacity, and the ability to reinforce losses gave colonial powers overwhelming long-term advantages. But the resistance was real, often prolonged, and sometimes spectacularly successful in the short term.

In Latin America, **Túpac Amaru II** (José Gabriel Condorcanqui) led the largest indigenous uprising in colonial history in 1780–81. Mobilizing tens of thousands of indigenous and mestizo people against Spanish taxation and forced labor (the *mita* system), his forces briefly threatened to overturn Spanish rule in Peru. The Spanish captured and executed him in 1781, his body publicly dismembered to terrorize potential rebels, but his name became a symbol of resistance for centuries afterward.

In India, the **1857 Rebellion** spread far beyond its origins in sepoy (soldier) resentment of East India Company policies. When soldiers refused to use new cartridges rumored to be greased with pig and cow fat (offensive to both Muslims and Hindus), the uprising expanded into a general rebellion involving peasants, landlords, and princes who had accumulated years of grievances. The rebels captured Delhi and proclaimed the restoration of Mughal rule. British forces reconquered Delhi after a prolonged siege, executed thousands, and used the rebellion to justify ending Company rule entirely.

In West Africa, **Samory Touré** built the Wassoulou Empire and used sophisticated guerrilla tactics, scorched earth strategy, mobile warfare, and even his own arms manufacturing, to resist French expansion for nearly three decades before his capture in 1898. In the Gold Coast (present-day Ghana), the Asante Queen Mother **Yaa Asantewaa** launched the Yaa Asantewaa War in 1900 after the British governor demanded the Asante surrender the Golden Stool, the sacred symbol of Asante sovereignty. “If you, the chiefs of Asante,” she reportedly declared, “will not go forward, then we will. We, the women, will. I shall call upon my fellow women.”

blocks.alt: Indigenous warriors resisting European colonial expansion
blocks.caption: Indigenous resistance to European colonial expansion took many forms, from large-scale military campaigns to guerrilla warfare to spiritual movements.
blocks.attribution: Most ultimately failed against industrialized military power (Google Gemini, 2025), commercially licensed.

blocks.text: The Battle of Isandlwana (January 22, 1879) was one of the worst defeats in British military history. About 20,000 Zulu warriors, armed primarily with spears, defeated 1,300 British soldiers equipped with rifles and artillery, by outflanking them and getting close enough that the rifles’ advantage was neutralized. The British public was stunned. Britain immediately sent 10,000 reinforcements, and Zululand was conquered by August 1879. One victory; one lost war.
🏛️ Creating New States: Building Power to Resist

The CED identifies a second pattern of response: indigenous communities created **new states on the periphery** of colonial expansion (KC-5.2.II.C). Rather than simply fighting off individual colonial advances, these communities built larger, more powerful political entities specifically to resist domination.

The **Sokoto Caliphate**, founded in 1804 by the Islamic scholar Usman dan Fodio in present-day Nigeria, unified dozens of fragmented Hausa city-states through the Fulani Jihad. By mid-century it was one of the largest states in Africa, with a population of perhaps 10 million and a sophisticated administrative structure. The Caliphate resisted European encroachment for decades before British conquest in 1903. Its survival into the 20th century demonstrated how political consolidation could significantly delay colonial conquest.

In southern Africa, the **Zulu Kingdom** under Shaka (r. 1816–28) expanded rapidly by incorporating neighboring peoples through a combination of conquest and alliance, creating a military force organized around age-grade regiments (*amabutho*). The Zulus defeated the British at Isandlwana (1879) before ultimately losing at Ulundi later that year.

The CED also notes Balkan nation-states as examples. Greece (independence 1821), Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, and others broke away from the weakening Ottoman Empire, demonstrating how nationalism enabled state formation in response to imperial decline. The **Cherokee Nation** in North America is another example: the Cherokee adopted a written constitution, established schools and newspapers, and attempted to build a recognizable “civilized” nation-state in hopes that demonstrating “civilized” status would protect them from removal. It did not, the Trail of Tears (1838) removed them anyway.

The CED identifies three specific types of indigenous responses for Topic 6.3: (1) direct resistance (Túpac Amaru II, Samory Touré, Yaa Asantewaa War, 1857 Rebellion in India), (2) new states on peripheries (Sokoto Caliphate, Cherokee Nation, Zulu Kingdom, Balkan states), and (3) religious/spiritual rebellions (Ghost Dance, Xhosa Cattle-Killing, Mahdist Wars). Know at least one specific example from each category for the exam.
🕊️ Religious and Spiritual Resistance: Faith Against Empire

When military options were exhausted or unavailable, communities often turned to religious and spiritual frameworks as forms of resistance. These movements combined genuine spiritual belief with political resistance to colonial rule, and the CED identifies them as a distinct category (KC-5.3.III.E): discontent produced rebellions influenced by religious ideas.

The **Ghost Dance** movement spread rapidly among Plains Indian peoples in 1889–90, inspired by the teachings of Wovoka, a Paiute prophet who had a vision during a solar eclipse. He taught that performing the Ghost Dance would cause European settlers to disappear, the land to regenerate, and the buffalo to return. The movement spread because it offered hope to communities that had been defeated militarily, stripped of their land, and confined to reservations. U.S. authorities, alarmed by the movement’s spread, attempted to arrest Sitting Bull, who was killed in the confrontation. The crisis culminated in the massacre at **Wounded Knee** (December 29, 1890), where U.S. soldiers killed approximately 300 Lakota Sioux, men, women, and children.

In southern Africa, the **Xhosa Cattle-Killing Movement** (1856–57) arose after a young woman named Nongqawuse received a prophecy: if the Xhosa killed all their cattle and destroyed their crops, the ancestors would rise, the Europeans would be driven into the sea, and the land would be restored. Desperate after years of warfare and cattle disease, thousands of Xhosa followed the prophecy. The result was catastrophic: without cattle or crops, Xhosa communities starved. Approximately 40,000 people died, and the Xhosa became dependent on colonial labor as their capacity for resistance collapsed. Well-intentioned religious belief, under conditions of extreme stress and despair, produced a self-defeating outcome.

In Sudan, the **Mahdist War** (1881–98) combined Islamic revival with anti-colonial resistance. Muhammad Ahmad declared himself the *Mahdi* (the “Expected One” in Islamic eschatology) and led a movement that defeated Egyptian-British forces, killed the famous British General Gordon at Khartoum (1885), and held Sudan independently for more than a decade. The Mahdist state was eventually destroyed at the Battle of Omdurman (1898), where Kitchener’s British forces, equipped with Maxim guns, killed over 11,000 Mahdist soldiers while suffering only 48 British deaths.

The Maxim gun, invented by Hiram Maxim in 1884, was the world’s first fully automatic machine gun. It could fire 500 rounds per minute. British poet Hilaire Belloc captured the colonial military asymmetry perfectly: “Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim Gun, and they have not.” At the Battle of Omdurman, 11,000 Mahdist soldiers died; 48 British soldiers did. Technology, not courage or moral superiority, determined the outcome.

multipleChoice.stimulus: “I shall call upon my fellow women. We, the women, will fight the Governor. If you, the men of Asante, will not go forward, then we will. We will fight till the last of us falls in the battlefields.”. Attributed to Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Asante, 1900
multipleChoice.question: The speech attributed to Yaa Asantewaa most directly exemplifies which pattern of indigenous response to colonial expansion?
options: Direct armed resistance to colonial conquest
The creation of a new state on the periphery of colonial expansion
Religious or spiritual resistance inspired by prophetic vision
Political accommodation by working within colonial governmental structures
multipleChoice.explanation: Yaa Asantewaa is calling for direct armed resistance. She is mobilizing the Asante to fight the British governor who demanded the Golden Stool, the sacred symbol of Asante sovereignty. The Yaa Asantewaa War (1900) is the CED’s illustrative example of direct resistance in West Africa. (C) No prophetic vision is mentioned. (B) The Asante Kingdom already existed; she wasn’t creating a new state. (D) She is explicitly calling for fighting, not accommodation.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "The Sokoto Caliphate, established in 1804 through the Fulani Jihad led by Usman dan Fodio, unified dozens of previously fragmented Hausa city-states under a single Islamic administrative structure. By 1850 it governed an estimated 10 million people and maintained a network of Islamic courts, scholarship, and governance that resisted European encroachment for nearly a century."
multipleChoice.question: The Sokoto Caliphate is best categorized as which type of indigenous response to the pressures of the imperial age?
options: Direct armed resistance modeled on European military organization
A religious resistance movement that rejected all political organization in favor of spiritual renewal
A new state created on the periphery that unified fragmented communities to resist colonial pressure
An accommodation strategy that sought to negotiate a protected status within European colonial law
multipleChoice.explanation: The Sokoto Caliphate is the CED’s primary example of a new state created on the periphery (KC-5.2.II.C). It unified fragmented Hausa states into a larger, more powerful political entity specifically organized around Islamic governance, creating the scale needed to resist colonial conquest for nearly a century. (A) is wrong, the Caliphate predated the main phase of European expansion in West Africa and was not modeled on European military organization. (B) is wrong, the Caliphate had a sophisticated political and legal structure. (D) is wrong, it was not an accommodation strategy.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "In 1889 and 1890, the Ghost Dance movement spread rapidly among Plains Indian peoples. The prophet Wovoka taught that performing the Ghost Dance would cause the earth to be renewed, the ancestors to return, the buffalo to come back, and the white settlers to disappear. The movement spread to peoples who had been militarily defeated, confined to reservations, and stripped of their traditional livelihoods."
multipleChoice.question: The rapid spread of the Ghost Dance among reservation communities is best explained by which of the following?
options: U.S. government policies that funded indigenous religious revival movements as a form of cultural reconciliation
Plains Indian peoples had traditionally embraced prophetic movements as the primary form of political organization
The Ghost Dance was originally a European Christian movement adapted by indigenous peoples
The movement offered hope to communities for whom conventional political and military resistance had been exhausted or defeated
multipleChoice.explanation: The passage explicitly notes that the movement spread among peoples “who had been militarily defeated, confined to reservations, and stripped of their traditional livelihoods”, communities for whom military and political options had been foreclosed. Spiritual movements that promise miraculous restoration are particularly appealing when material options have been exhausted. This is the CED’s KC-5.3.III.E: rebellions influenced by religious ideas emerge from discontent when other forms of resistance are unavailable. (A) is historically inaccurate, the U.S. government actively suppressed the Ghost Dance. (C) is false. (B) is an overgeneralization.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "The Cherokee Nation adopted a written constitution in 1827, established a bilingual newspaper, built schools on the European model, and conducted formal diplomacy with the U.S. government, all in the belief that demonstrating ‘civilized’ status would protect them from removal. In 1838, the U.S. Army forcibly relocated 15,000 Cherokee to Indian Territory on the Trail of Tears; approximately 4,000 died during the removal."
multipleChoice.question: The Cherokee Nation’s strategy and its outcome best illustrates which historical argument?
options: Indigenous accommodation strategies were always more effective than direct military resistance
Colonial expansion was driven by racial and economic interests that indigenous political adaptation could not overcome
The U.S. government consistently honored treaty obligations with indigenous nations when they complied with American cultural expectations
The civilizing mission ideology was consistently applied to protect indigenous peoples who adopted European practices
multipleChoice.explanation: The Cherokee adopted every strategy that the civilizing mission ideology supposedly rewarded, literacy, constitutionalism, schools, formal diplomacy, yet were forcibly removed anyway. This demonstrates that the civilizing mission was ideological cover for expansion, not a genuine policy of protecting “civilized” indigenous peoples. The actual drivers, land hunger and racial hierarchy, overrode cultural performance. (A) is contradicted by the passage. (C) is historically inaccurate. (D) is directly contradicted by the outcome described.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "At the Battle of Omdurman (1898), Kitchener’s British and Egyptian forces killed approximately 11,000 Mahdist soldiers while suffering 48 British deaths. The primary British advantage was the Maxim gun, which could fire 500 rounds per minute. Hilaire Belloc later wrote: ‘Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim Gun, and they have not.’"
multipleChoice.question: The outcome of the Battle of Omdurman most directly supports which conclusion about anticolonial resistance in the late 19th century?
options: African military forces lacked the organizational discipline needed to resist European armies effectively
Religious motivation was insufficient to produce effective military strategy
The industrial military-technology gap between colonial and colonized societies was the decisive factor limiting the effectiveness of armed resistance
British imperial expansion in Africa was primarily driven by military adventurism rather than economic or ideological goals
multipleChoice.explanation: A 230:1 casualty ratio is not explained by organizational discipline, courage, or strategy. It reflects the overwhelming advantage of industrial weapons (Maxim gun, modern artillery) over pre-industrial military technology. Belloc’s lines make the point explicitly: the decisive variable was technology, not character. (A) is wrong and condescending, the Mahdist army had successfully organized and defeated major forces for 17 years; the Battle of Omdurman was lost to technology, not disorganization. (B) conflates religious motivation with strategic effectiveness. (D) is not supported by the passage.

saq.context: “Indigenous peoples did not passively accept colonial conquest. They responded through a spectrum of strategies, from armed resistance and new state-building to religious movements and political accommodation. Most ultimately failed to prevent conquest, but the resistance itself shaped colonial policy, created lasting historical memories, and demonstrated the agency of colonized peoples.”
saq.directions: Answer parts A, B, and C. Each requires a separate short response. Do not write a full essay.

parts.label: Part A
parts.task: Briefly describe ONE specific example of direct armed resistance to colonial expansion from 1750 to 1900, and explain why it ultimately failed.
parts.sampleAnswer: The 1857 Rebellion in India began when sepoys refused to use cartridges rumored to be greased with pig and cow fat, but spread into a general uprising against East India Company rule involving civilians, landlords, and princes across northern India. Rebels captured Delhi and proclaimed the restoration of Mughal rule. The rebellion ultimately failed because Britain could reinforce its forces from the global empire while the rebels lacked coordinated leadership, access to industrial weapons, and a unified political vision. Britain’s ability to absorb the initial setback and return with overwhelming force exemplifies why armed resistance against industrial military power was structurally difficult to sustain, regardless of the courage or determination of those resisting.

parts.label: Part B
parts.task: Briefly explain ONE way the Ghost Dance movement or the Xhosa Cattle-Killing Movement represents a form of resistance to colonial expansion.
parts.sampleAnswer: The Ghost Dance was a direct response to colonial conquest: it emerged among Plains Indian peoples who had been militarily defeated, stripped of their land, confined to reservations, and deprived of the buffalo that had sustained their economies. The movement’s promise, that performing the ritual would restore indigenous life and remove settlers, was a form of resistance in that it rejected the permanence of colonial conquest and asserted indigenous people’s right to reclaim their world. The U.S. government’s alarm at the movement’s spread and its violent suppression at Wounded Knee demonstrate that colonial authorities recognized it as a threat to social control, even though it was a spiritual rather than military movement.

parts.label: Part C
parts.task: Briefly explain ONE way a new state created in the 19th century (such as the Sokoto Caliphate or Zulu Kingdom) served as a form of resistance to colonial expansion.
parts.sampleAnswer: The Sokoto Caliphate, founded in 1804 in present-day Nigeria, unified dozens of fragmented Hausa city-states under a single Islamic administrative and legal framework. This political consolidation created a state with a population of approximately 10 million, a sophisticated governance structure, and the military and economic resources to resist European encroachment for nearly a century. By centralizing political authority and providing a shared ideological framework (Islam), the Caliphate converted what would have been fragmented, easily defeated local resistance into sustained regional resistance. It was not conquered until 1903, demonstrating how state-building could significantly extend the capacity to resist colonial expansion beyond what scattered communities could achieve individually.

outline.label: Evidence for limited effectiveness
outline.text: Battle of Omdurman (1898): 11,000 Mahdist killed vs. 48 British, technology gap is decisive; 1857 Rebellion: spectacular initial success, total defeat within 2 years; Xhosa Cattle-Killing: spiritual resistance led to catastrophic self-destruction; Cherokee Nation: total adoption of “civilized” norms did not prevent Trail of Tears

outline.label: Evidence for some effectiveness (qualification)
outline.text: Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa (1896), remained independent until 1935; Samory Touré delayed French conquest for nearly 30 years through guerrilla tactics; Resistance shaped colonial policy: 1857 changed British governance of India permanently; Mahdist state held Sudan independently for 17 years; Zulu defeat of British at Isandlwana slowed conquest and temporarily reversed it

outline.label: Contextualization
outline.text: Industrial Revolution created military technology gap; ideological justifications (Topic 6.1) made resistance appear as obstacles to “progress” rather than legitimate political opposition.

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which indigenous resistance to colonial expansion from 1750 to 1900 was effective in limiting or reversing the growth of European empires.
leq.note: Write a full essay with a thesis, contextualization, evidence, and historical reasoning. Use causation or argumentation as your primary skill. A strong response will acknowledge both the genuine power of resistance and the structural factors that ultimately limited its effectiveness.
leq.thesisExample: Strong thesis: “Although indigenous resistance to colonial expansion was widespread, creative, and sometimes militarily significant in the short term, it was largely ineffective in preventing conquest in the long run because the military-technology gap created by industrialization, particularly the Maxim gun, modern artillery, and steamships, gave colonial powers an overwhelming structural advantage that no amount of courage, political organization, or spiritual conviction could overcome.”

discussionQuestions.question: 1. The Xhosa Cattle-Killing Movement ended in catastrophe for the Xhosa people. Does this mean it was irrational? How should historians judge the choices people make under conditions of extreme desperation?
discussionQuestions.modelAnswer: Judging historical decisions requires understanding the context in which they were made, not just the outcomes. By 1856, the Xhosa had fought and lost four major wars with the British Cape Colony; their cattle had been devastated by a lung disease; their land was being seized; and their political autonomy was collapsing. From within that context, a prophetic promise of miraculous restoration wasn’t simply irrational. It was one of the very few options that seemed to offer any hope at all. Human beings under catastrophic stress frequently turn to frameworks that offer explanation and hope; the Xhosa were no different from the Plains Indians who joined the Ghost Dance or the Judeans who joined messianic movements under Roman occupation. The question isn’t whether the prophecy was true but whether the decision to follow it was understandable given the options available.

discussionQuestions.question: 2. The 1857 Rebellion in India failed to expel the British but permanently changed British colonial policy. How can a failed resistance movement still have significant historical consequences?
discussionQuestions.modelAnswer: Military failure and historical insignificance are not the same thing. The 1857 Rebellion failed to achieve its immediate goal, British expulsion, but it fundamentally transformed British rule in India. It ended the East India Company’s governance and transferred India to direct Crown control. It made British administrators more cautious about intervening in Indian social and religious practices (the cartridge incident had revealed how deeply such interventions could provoke resistance). It preserved the memory of armed resistance and became foundational to Indian nationalist consciousness in the 20th century. Mohandas Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru both invoked 1857 as a precursor to independence. A failed rebellion can reshape policy, create martyrs, establish historical memory, and lay the ideological groundwork for later movements that succeed.

discussionQuestions.question: 3. The CED identifies three categories of indigenous response: direct resistance, new states, and religious/spiritual movements. What does the existence of all three categories suggest about how colonial expansion affected indigenous societies?
discussionQuestions.modelAnswer: The three categories reflect the range of resources, military, political, and spiritual, that communities mobilized when facing existential threat. Not every community had the same options: some had enough military strength to fight; others had enough political sophistication to build new state structures; others turned to spiritual resources when material ones were unavailable. The existence of all three categories also suggests that indigenous peoples were not passive victims but active agents who analyzed their situations and chose strategies based on available means. The fact that most ultimately failed does not erase the agency involved. It reflects the structural asymmetry of industrial versus pre-industrial military power, not the absence of resistance.
